questions.text: A university wants to publish survey data but risks exposing respondents because the sample is small. Which revision offers a defensible balance?
options: Publish every response because transparency always overrides privacy.
Release only aggregate results with protective thresholds and explain the resulting limits on analysis.
Suppress all findings without explaining why.
Publish names but omit the survey questions.
questions.explanation: Aggregating and withholding potentially identifying small cells can protect confidentiality while communicating useful findings and their limitations.

questions.text: A journal changes from single-blind to double-blind review and claims it reduced prestige bias. What evidence would most directly support the claim?
options: A list of reviewers' favorite scientific topics.
The journal's higher annual submission count.
The length of reviewer instructions.
Changes in review-score disparities associated with author prestige, controlling for manuscript characteristics.
questions.explanation: Prestige-related score disparities conditional on article quality directly test the proposed bias reduction.

questions.text: A proposal to expand a journal's new manuscript-review checklist faces this objection: reviewers report greater administrative burden. Which response keeps a defensible argument without dismissing the concern?
options: The expense matters, but a journal's new manuscript-review checklist has already been discussed widely enough that measuring outcomes is unnecessary.
Because the program is intended to help, its costs and risks should not be weighed in the decision.
Although reviewers report greater administrative burden, a restricted pilot that measures the proportion of published corrections could show whether expansion is justified.
The concern could be reduced by delaying the decision, even if the program's effect on the proportion of published corrections is never measured.
questions.explanation: The strongest response acknowledges the specific burden while proposing evidence about the proportion of published corrections. The alternatives appeal to publicity, intentions, or postponement without addressing effectiveness and cost together.

questions.text: In the day 19 psychology full-paper case: Which additional method would most reduce uncertainty about a causal claim in psychology?
options: Repeat the same conclusion in several paragraphs.
Remove inconvenient outliers without documenting them.
Identify selection effects and plausible confounding variables.
Replace the results section with a more confident abstract.
questions.explanation: Addressing confounding and selection can distinguish a causal relationship from a misleading association.

questions.text: A paragraph reports encouraging initial results for a journal's new manuscript-review checklist. The next explains that the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening. Which transition and qualification best connect the paragraphs?
options: Nevertheless, the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening, so the effect of the program itself remains uncertain.
Furthermore, the timing of the competing change demonstrates that the new program produced the entire benefit.
By contrast, the competing change establishes that the program had no effect at all.
Consequently, additional evidence is unnecessary because both changes occurred in the same period.
questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless' marks a limitation to positive findings and preserves uncertainty about the competing change. The other options assert proof of benefit or ineffectiveness or dismiss the need for comparison.

questions.text: In the day 19 psychology full-paper case: Which finding would independently corroborate a disputed historical claim in psychology?
options: An unrelated dated record supports the same chronology.
The original author repeats the claim in a later paragraph.
Several summaries quote the same anonymous assertion.
A popular account asserts the story is interesting.
questions.explanation: Independent supporting material is stronger corroboration than restating the same unsupported source.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 scientific publishing assessment, What unstated assumption is required to infer public opinion from a volunteer survey?
options: The reviewers interviewed every official.
The volunteers adequately represent the wider population.
All respondents prefer answering surveys.
The survey paper contains at least two paragraphs.
questions.explanation: Extrapolating from volunteers assumes they do not differ systematically from the broader public.

questions.text: Observed the proportion of published corrections changed after a journal's new manuscript-review checklist began. At the same time, the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening. Which interpretation avoids a post hoc fallacy?
options: Any favorable change following the launch must have resulted from the program.
The timing is compatible with an effect, but it cannot isolate the program from the concurrent change.
The concurrent change proves the program was irrelevant in every setting.
Since both changes occurred together, they must have had exactly equal effects.
questions.explanation: The observation alone cannot separate simultaneous causes. The first interpretation preserves the association while recognizing the alternate explanation; the other options infer necessity, absence, or equal effects without evidence.

questions.text: Opponents of a journal's new manuscript-review checklist argue that the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening may distort the findings. Which response fairly represents the concern before answering it?
options: Opponents claim that no observation can ever be trusted, so their view deserves no attention.
The concern is that the competing circumstance may explain some of the measured change; a matched comparison can test that.
The competing circumstance proves every observed benefit is imaginary.
The concern is merely about the popularity of the program, not about evidence.
questions.explanation: A fair response states the real methodological concern and proposes a way to examine it, unlike exaggerations that distort or dismiss the objection.

questions.text: A critic says a journal's new manuscript-review checklist may have uncertain effects because the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening. Which reply avoids misrepresenting the objection?
options: The objection concerns the ability to separate causes, so we should measure the competing change before drawing conclusions.
The critic believes every program should be banned permanently.
The critic rejects all evidence that could ever support the program.
The critic is opposed to helping the people served by the program.
questions.explanation: The correct response answers the actual causal concern. The alternatives substitute extreme claims about the critic's values or beliefs.

questions.text: A council attributes changes in the proportion of published corrections to a journal's new manuscript-review checklist. Which evidence would most directly evaluate this causal claim?
options: The number of promotional materials distributed when the project started.
An opinion survey among only those who chose to enroll after the announcement.
Comparable before-and-after outcome measures, with baseline differences and the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening accounted for.
A count of project meetings, without any recorded the proportion of published corrections.
questions.explanation: Outcome measures with appropriate comparison and confounder accounting directly address the alleged improvement. Promotion, selective opinions and meeting totals are weak substitutes for the claimed outcome.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 scientific publishing assessment, What most directly addresses external validity after a promising result in one institution?
options: An additional summary of the same initial observations.
Removing participants who disagree with the reviewer's conclusion.
Replication in institutions with different populations and operating conditions.
A larger poster advertising the first trial.
questions.explanation: External validity concerns whether findings hold across relevant settings and populations.

questions.text: One paragraph reports encouraging changes in the proportion of published corrections; the next considers the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening. Which opening makes the relationship clear?
options: Furthermore, the competing circumstance demonstrates the program was the sole cause.
Similarly, the complication proves every finding is false.
Therefore, causal uncertainty can be ignored because the outcome was favorable.
Nevertheless, the competing circumstance limits any immediate claim that the program alone caused the improvement.
questions.explanation: Nevertheless marks a qualification to favorable evidence and states what remains uncertain. The other transitions turn concurrent changes into unjustified proof.

questions.text: A student is writing a policy essay about a journal's new manuscript-review checklist. Which thesis is both contestable and specific enough to evaluate?
options: There are many views about the program, some supportive and some critical.
This essay will discuss several possible aspects of the proposed program.
The program is good because well-intentioned people have recommended it.
A limited expansion should be considered if measured gains in the proportion of published corrections justify costs after accounting for competing explanations.
questions.explanation: The first thesis advocates a concrete conditional policy grounded in outcomes and costs. The other statements merely announce a topic, summarize opinions, or rely on intentions rather than evaluable reasoning.

questions.text: Two explanations fit an observed shift in the proportion of published corrections: the launch of a journal's new manuscript-review checklist and the fact that the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening. Which next measurement best distinguishes them?
options: Collect additional testimonials from people who already believe the program worked.
Repeat the preferred explanation in the report's conclusion.
Compare similar groups with differing exposure to the program while measuring the competing change.
Measure the launch date more precisely without collecting any outcome data.
questions.explanation: A comparison varying exposure while tracking the rival factor tests divergent causal predictions. Testimonials, repetition and precise launch dates alone do not discriminate explanations.

questions.text: A review seeks to estimate whether a journal's new manuscript-review checklist altered the proportion of published corrections. Which approach supplies the most defensible counterfactual?
options: Compare the participants' comments only after the program has ended.
Compare suitably matched participants or sites with and without the program, adjusting for baseline outcome differences.
Use the program's stated objective as evidence that it reached that objective.
Measure only the most successful pilot site and generalize to every site.
questions.explanation: A matched comparison with baseline adjustment can approximate what would have happened without the intervention. Selection based on success and opinions or intentions cannot establish the counterfactual.

questions.text: A sponsor claims a journal's new manuscript-review checklist produced a lasting improvement in the proportion of published corrections. Which assessment most fairly evaluates the sponsor's evidence?
options: Inspect the sampling method, underlying outcome data, and independent replication while checking the competing change.
Accept the claim if the sponsor has a prestigious professional title.
Reject the claim without examination because the source has a financial interest.
Count how many different websites repeat the sponsor's press release.
questions.explanation: Evaluating methods, records and independent evidence addresses both credibility and possible bias. Reputation, automatic dismissal, and repetitive citation alone are not sufficient tests.

questions.text: An archived local report describes a journal's new manuscript-review checklist at one site in a particular year. Which historical inference is warranted without additional records?
options: The program must have been identical at every institution in the country.
The archived description proves every participant supported the program.
The presence of one report establishes its effectiveness throughout the entire period.
The program was documented at that site, but its prevalence or effects elsewhere remain uncertain.
questions.explanation: One record can document existence in its own context but cannot establish geographic prevalence, universal attitudes, or effectiveness without corroboration.

questions.text: A writer compares an initial pilot of a journal's new manuscript-review checklist with a trial of a new school schedule. When would the analogy offer meaningful evidence for expansion?
options: When both initiatives were announced in the same season, regardless of their mechanisms.
When their titles sound similar even if the intended users differ.
When both pilots share relevant constraints, comparable target groups, and outcomes measured against plausible alternatives.
When the school trial was popular, even if it never measured any outcome.
questions.explanation: Analogies support inference when the features bearing on the conclusion are shared. Superficial timing, naming, and popularity do not establish comparable mechanisms or outcomes.

questions.text: A report identifies an encouraging change in the proportion of published corrections but cannot separate a journal's new manuscript-review checklist from the competing circumstance that the journal simultaneously tightened desk screening. Which conclusion best synthesizes the evidence?
options: The positive change proves that every participant benefited exclusively from the program.
The observations justify targeted follow-up, but a program-specific causal benefit remains unconfirmed.
The competing circumstance disproves the existence of any possible program benefit.
No preliminary description of the outcome is permissible while uncertainty remains.
questions.explanation: The first synthesis reports the observation and a reasonable next step while retaining causal uncertainty. The alternatives overgeneralize, deny possible effects, or refuse to describe valid limited evidence.

questions.text: Which revision keeps the two steps in parallel active voice while identifying the same actor?
options: The linguists transcribed each recording, and the samples were compared.
Each recording was transcribed by the linguists, and they compared the samples.
The linguists transcribed each recording and compared the samples.
Transcribing each recording, the samples were compared.
questions.explanation: Both active predicates 'transcribed' and 'compared' have the plural subject 'linguists', improving parallelism and avoiding the dangling phrase in option D.

questions.text: Each of the analysts who evaluated supplemental bilingual instruction ___ responsible for a separate written report. Choose the formal singular verb.
options: are
have
were
is
questions.explanation: Each is the singular grammatical head and takes is despite plural analysts in the intervening phrase.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: By the time Daniel presented the finding, the review team ___ its sources.
options: will check
is checking
had already checked
has already checked
questions.explanation: Past perfect marks a completed event before another past event.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: After reviewing the contradictory evidence, ___.
options: a discrepancy became apparent
the finding was amended
the result seemed doubtful
the specialists revised their interpretation
questions.explanation: The people who performed the reviewing must immediately follow the opening modifier.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: The revised interpretation was more comprehensive than ___.
options: that in the earlier finding
the previous chair
the original specialists
the archive that stored the document
questions.explanation: The construction compares interpretations with interpretations, not people or institutions.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: If Daniel ___ responsible for the finding, the chair would seek independent confirmation.
options: is
were
will be
has been
questions.explanation: Were expresses an unreal present condition in conventional formal usage.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: The finding may be accepted only if the specialists approve it. What can be inferred?
options: Acceptance may precede approval under the stated rule.
No unapproved measure has ever been submitted.
Their approval is necessary, not necessarily sufficient.
Their approval guarantees acceptance.
questions.explanation: Only if specifies a necessary condition and does not guarantee success.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: Which sentence identifies Daniel as the person who actually inspected the evidence?
options: Daniel informed the chair after she inspected it.
After she inspected it, Daniel informed the chair.
The chair and Daniel discussed the findings after she inspected it.
After inspecting the evidence, Daniel informed the chair.
questions.explanation: The participial phrase 'After inspecting the evidence' directly modifies the named person who performed the inspection. The alternatives contain ambiguous pronouns or less clearly attach the action to its agent.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: Which sentence means that the specialists revised no section except the conclusion?
options: The specialists revised only the conclusion of the finding.
Only the specialists revised the conclusion of the finding.
The specialists only revised the conclusion of the finding.
The specialists revised the only conclusion of the finding.
questions.explanation: Only immediately before the object narrows what was revised.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: Which sentence correctly connects two independent clauses with a conjunctive adverb?
options: The finding was persuasive nevertheless; the chair requested more evidence.
The finding was persuasive; nevertheless, the chair requested more evidence.
The finding was persuasive, nevertheless, the chair requested more evidence.
The finding was persuasive; nevertheless the chair requested more evidence.
questions.explanation: A semicolon separates the independent clauses and a comma follows nevertheless.

questions.text: A number of analysts working on supplemental bilingual instruction ___ requested a second independent review.
options: has
is
have
was
questions.explanation: A number of is a plural quantifier phrase and takes have; by contrast, 'the number of' is singular.

questions.text: The revised language report showed a decline in the number of coding mistakes but also in the amount of ambiguity. Which pair of quantifiers correctly completes the sentence: 'There were ___ coding mistakes and ___ ambiguity'?
options: less; fewer
fewer; less
fewer; fewer
less; less
questions.explanation: The plural count noun requires 'fewer', while the mass noun takes 'less'. Reversing them or applying one form to both ignores the count-versus-quantity distinction.

questions.text: Several investigators evaluating supplemental bilingual instruction ___ questioned the original conclusion.
options: have
has
is
was
questions.explanation: Several is a plural quantifier and governs the plural auxiliary have. The singular verbs fail to agree with the head.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Either the specialists or the department head ___ required to approve the final finding.
options: have
is
are
were
questions.explanation: The nearest noun head is singular, so is is correct.

questions.text: Which version correctly joins two complete observations about the language survey?
options: The linguists recorded coding mistakes, one recording was damaged.
The linguists recorded coding mistakes; one recording was damaged.
The linguists recorded coding mistakes; and, one recording was damaged.
The linguists recorded coding mistakes: and one recording was damaged.
questions.explanation: The semicolon joins two related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. The comma-only version splices clauses, while the other versions misuse punctuation with 'and'.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Which construction uses inversion correctly after the negative adverbial?
options: Not only the oversight board did revise its measure, but explained also.
Not only did the oversight board revised its measure but also explained.
Not only the oversight board had revised its measure, but it also explaining.
Not only did the oversight board revise its measure, but it also explained the change.
questions.explanation: Negative-initial not only requires auxiliary inversion in the first clause.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly identifies the researcher who owns the data table used in the review of supplemental bilingual instruction?
options: The researcher whose data table was audited supplied a new copy.
The researcher who's data table was audited supplied a new copy.
The researcher whom's data table was audited supplied a new copy.
The researcher who data table was audited supplied a new copy.
questions.explanation: Whose expresses possession in a relative clause; who's means who is or who has, and the other forms do not serve as possessives.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Which sentence means that the director considered just one document and no others?
options: The director examined the only revised finding.
The director examined only the revised finding.
Only the director examined the revised finding.
The director only examined the revised finding.
questions.explanation: Only modifies the immediately following object 'the revised finding' to restrict the documents examined.

questions.text: A report compares transcription accuracy in the language survey and the previous survey. Which sentence correctly compares the measures rather than a measure with a project?
options: The transcription accuracy of the language survey was higher than the previous survey.
The transcription accuracy of the language survey was higher than that of the previous survey.
The transcription accuracy of the language survey was higher than the authors of the previous survey.
The transcription accuracy of the language survey was more higher than the previous survey.
questions.explanation: 'That of' substitutes for the corresponding measurement in the other project. The distractors compare unlike entities or use an ungrammatical double comparative.

questions.text: The team found a smaller quantity of ambiguity and a smaller number of coding mistakes. Which sentence describes both changes with appropriate quantifiers?
options: The team recorded fewer ambiguity and less coding mistakes.
The team recorded less ambiguity and fewer coding mistakes.
The team recorded less ambiguity and less coding mistakes.
The team recorded fewer ambiguity and fewer coding mistakes.
questions.explanation: 'Less' modifies the uncountable quantity and 'fewer' modifies the countable plural. All other combinations misapply at least one quantifier.

questions.text: The linguists had ___ transcribing the oral histories.
options: begun
began
begin
beginned
questions.explanation: Begun is the past participle after had, unlike the simple past began. Other choices have an incorrect form, meaning, or syntactic role in this context.

questions.text: The sample population ___ residents of five language districts.
options: composes
comprises
comprised
composed
questions.explanation: Comprises means includes; composes indicates a different relationship. Other choices have an incorrect form, meaning, or syntactic role in this context.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Which sentence consistently reports a past claim without an illogical tense shift?
options: The editor said that the oversight board review the evidence before it published.
The editor said that the oversight board had reviews the evidence before publishing.
The editor said that the oversight board had reviewed the evidence before publishing.
The editor said that the oversight board will have reviewed the evidence yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past reporting combines naturally with a past perfect for an earlier action.

questions.text: The report has already identified Ms. Perez. Which sentence treats the additional information about this named person as nonessential?
options: Ms. Perez who inspected the recording device, submitted the findings.
Ms. Perez, who inspected the recording device, submitted the findings.
Ms. Perez, who inspected the recording device submitted the findings.
Ms. Perez who inspected the recording device submitted, the findings.
questions.explanation: A supplementary who-clause about an already identified person takes commas on both sides. The other versions omit or misplace a clause boundary.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Which version makes the introductory action's agent unambiguous?
options: Having reviewed the transcript, the historian corrected the chronology.
Having reviewed the transcript, the chronology was corrected.
After studying the archive, a discrepancy appeared.
Having read the transcript, the finding's conclusions changed.
questions.explanation: The historian is the following subject and therefore performs the reviewing.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Which version appropriately uses were to express an unreal present condition?
options: The oversight board spoke as if the outcome be already certainty.
The oversight board spoke as if the outcome were already certain.
The oversight board spoke as if the outcome will already certain.
The oversight board spoke as if the outcome had certain yesterday.
questions.explanation: Were marks a contrary-to-fact or hypothetical state in formal usage.

questions.text: Neither of the two interpretations offered for the language survey ___ supported by the available record. Which verb agrees with the singular distributive subject?
options: are
is
were
have
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is singular in this formal construction, so it takes 'is' rather than a plural verb, regardless of the plural noun in the modifying phrase.

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, Which question correctly uses whom in a formal object position?
options: Whom submitted the final finding?
Whom was responsible for the analysis?
Whom have been approved for the hearing?
Whom did the panel invite to testify?
questions.explanation: Whom is the object of invite; the other questions need subject-case who.

questions.text: Which version correctly punctuates an introductory dependent clause explaining a decision about the language survey?
options: Although one recording was damaged the linguists, reviewed the evidence.
Although one recording was damaged, the linguists reviewed the evidence.
Although, one recording was damaged the linguists reviewed the evidence.
Although one recording was damaged, and the linguists reviewed the evidence.
questions.explanation: The initial subordinate clause is followed by a comma before the main clause. The other choices misplace the comma or add an ungrammatical conjunction.

questions.text: Which sentence uses parallel objects after 'not only ... but also' when describing the language survey?
options: The linguists examined not only the dialect notes but also analyzing the language report.
The linguists examined not only the dialect notes but also the language report.
The linguists examined not only the dialect notes but also to evaluate the language report.
The linguists examined not only the dialect notes but also that the language report was correct.
questions.explanation: Both objects are parallel noun phrases governed by 'examined'. The alternatives shift to a participial, infinitival, or finite clause complement.

questions.text: Which word is misspelled?
options: wisdom
zealous
science
No mistakes.
questions.explanation: All three words are spelled correctly. Recall the standard forms: wisdom, zealous, science.

questions.text: Which word is misspelled?
options: withdrawl
authority
Wednesday
No mistakes.
questions.explanation: The misspelled form is withdrawl. Correct spelling: withdrawal. Divide the word into parts, identify the less obvious vowel sounds, and spell it again from memory.

questions.text: Which word is misspelled?
options: critique
writen

questions.text: A proposal to expand supplemental bilingual instruction faces this objection: teachers need additional training time. Which response keeps a defensible argument without dismissing the concern?

questions.text: A paragraph reports encouraging initial results for supplemental bilingual instruction. The next explains that participating families volunteered more home-reading time. Which transition and qualification best connect the paragraphs?

By contrast, the competing change establishes that the program had no effect at all.
Consequently, additional evidence is unnecessary because both changes occurred in the same period.
Nevertheless, participating families volunteered more home-reading time, so the effect of the program itself remains uncertain.
questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless' marks a limitation to positive findings and preserves uncertainty about the competing change. The other options assert proof of benefit or ineffectiveness or dismiss the need for comparison.

questions.text: In the day 20 urban history full-paper case: Which finding would independently corroborate a disputed historical claim in urban history?

questions.text: For a grade 10–12 linguistic analysis assessment, What unstated assumption is required to infer public opinion from a volunteer survey?

questions.text: Observed students' reading comprehension in both languages changed after supplemental bilingual instruction began. At the same time, participating families volunteered more home-reading time. Which interpretation avoids a post hoc fallacy?
options: The timing is compatible with an effect, but it cannot isolate the program from the concurrent change.
Any favorable change following the launch must have resulted from the program.
The concurrent change proves the program was irrelevant in every setting.
Since both changes occurred together, they must have had exactly equal effects.
questions.explanation: The observation alone cannot separate simultaneous causes. The first interpretation preserves the association while recognizing the alternate explanation; the other options infer necessity, absence, or equal effects without evidence.

questions.text: Opponents of supplemental bilingual instruction argue that participating families volunteered more home-reading time may distort the findings. Which response fairly represents the concern before answering it?

The competing circumstance proves every observed benefit is imaginary.
The concern is that the competing circumstance may explain some of the measured change; a matched comparison can test that.
The concern is merely about the popularity of the program, not about evidence.
questions.explanation: A fair response states the real methodological concern and proposes a way to examine it, unlike exaggerations that distort or dismiss the objection.

questions.text: A critic says supplemental bilingual instruction may have uncertain effects because participating families volunteered more home-reading time. Which reply avoids misrepresenting the objection?
options: The critic believes every program should be banned permanently.
The objection concerns the ability to separate causes, so we should measure the competing change before drawing conclusions.
The critic rejects all evidence that could ever support the program.
The critic is opposed to helping the people served by the program.
questions.explanation: The correct response answers the actual causal concern. The alternatives substitute extreme claims about the critic's values or beliefs.

questions.text: A council attributes changes in students' reading comprehension in both languages to supplemental bilingual instruction. Which evidence would most directly evaluate this causal claim?

Comparable before-and-after outcome measures, with baseline differences and participating families volunteered more home-reading time accounted for.
An opinion survey among only those who chose to enroll after the announcement.
A count of project meetings, without any recorded students' reading comprehension in both languages.
questions.explanation: Outcome measures with appropriate comparison and confounder accounting directly address the alleged improvement. Promotion, selective opinions and meeting totals are weak substitutes for the claimed outcome.

questions.text: Positive results for supplemental bilingual instruction came from a small, self-selected sample. What most directly tests whether they apply to the intended wider population?

Recruit a representative set of users across relevant backgrounds and measure comparable outcomes.
questions.explanation: Representative recruitment and comparable outcomes address external validity. More observations from the same biased frame do not necessarily do so.

questions.text: One paragraph reports encouraging changes in students' reading comprehension in both languages; the next considers participating families volunteered more home-reading time. Which opening makes the relationship clear?
options: Nevertheless, the competing circumstance limits any immediate claim that the program alone caused the improvement.
Furthermore, the competing circumstance demonstrates the program was the sole cause.
Similarly, the complication proves every finding is false.
Therefore, causal uncertainty can be ignored because the outcome was favorable.
questions.explanation: Nevertheless marks a qualification to favorable evidence and states what remains uncertain. The other transitions turn concurrent changes into unjustified proof.

questions.text: A student is writing a policy essay about supplemental bilingual instruction. Which thesis is both contestable and specific enough to evaluate?

The program is good because well-intentioned people have recommended it.
questions.explanation: The first thesis advocates a concrete conditional policy grounded in outcomes and costs. The other statements merely announce a topic, summarize opinions, or rely on intentions rather than evaluable reasoning.

questions.text: Two explanations fit an observed shift in students' reading comprehension in both languages: the launch of supplemental bilingual instruction and the fact that participating families volunteered more home-reading time. Which next measurement best distinguishes them?

Compare similar groups with differing exposure to the program while measuring the competing change.
Repeat the preferred explanation in the report's conclusion.
Measure the launch date more precisely without collecting any outcome data.
questions.explanation: A comparison varying exposure while tracking the rival factor tests divergent causal predictions. Testimonials, repetition and precise launch dates alone do not discriminate explanations.

questions.text: A review seeks to estimate whether supplemental bilingual instruction altered students' reading comprehension in both languages. Which approach supplies the most defensible counterfactual?

Compare the participants' comments only after the program has ended.
Use the program's stated objective as evidence that it reached that objective.
Measure only the most successful pilot site and generalize to every site.
questions.explanation: A matched comparison with baseline adjustment can approximate what would have happened without the intervention. Selection based on success and opinions or intentions cannot establish the counterfactual.

questions.text: A sponsor claims supplemental bilingual instruction produced a lasting improvement in students' reading comprehension in both languages. Which assessment most fairly evaluates the sponsor's evidence?

questions.explanation: Evaluating methods, records and independent evidence addresses both credibility and possible bias. Reputation, automatic dismissal, and repetitive citation alone are not sufficient tests.
